title: Scarcity
in30Seconds: Scarcity is the basic economic problem: the resources we have are limited, but our wants for goods and services are effectively unlimited. Because we can never produce enough to satisfy every want, every person, business, and government is forced to choose what to make and what to give up. That permanent gap between limited means and competing ends is the reason the field of economics exists at all.
whyItMatters: Scarcity is the starting point for almost every idea in economics. Once you see that resources are finite while wants are not, choice and tradeoffs stop being optional and become unavoidable, which is why the subject studies how people and societies decide. Recognizing scarcity also sharpens everyday reasoning: it explains why time budgets feel tight, why prices exist, and why 'we should just make more' is rarely a complete answer. Students who grasp scarcity clearly can then build toward choice, opportunity cost, incentives, and supply and demand without confusing a permanent condition with a temporary market glitch.
learningObjectives: Define scarcity as the gap between limited resources and unlimited or competing wants.
Explain why scarcity forces every individual and society to make choices and tradeoffs.
Identify and describe the four factors of production: land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship.
Distinguish scarcity, a permanent and universal condition, from a shortage, a temporary market condition.
Apply the idea of scarcity to an everyday situation, including so-called free goods and time.

collegeVersion.heading: Scarcity: the fundamental economic problem
collegeVersion.body: Economics begins with a simple, stubborn fact: there is not enough of everything to go around. The resources available to produce goods and services exist in limited supply, while human wants are, for practical purposes, unlimited. Put those two observations together and you get scarcity, the condition in which wants exceed the means available to satisfy them. Scarcity is not a temporary inconvenience or a sign that someone planned badly. It is a permanent feature of economic life that applies to individuals, firms, and entire nations alike. Because resources are limited, the quantity of goods and services we can produce with them is also limited, and no economy has ever produced enough to satisfy every want of every person. This gap is exactly why economics exists as a field. If everyone could have everything they wanted at no cost, there would be no need to study how people allocate resources, because no allocation decision would matter. Scarcity forces a decision at every turn: because you cannot have it all, choosing to use resources one way means not using them another way. That is why scarcity leads directly to choice, tradeoffs, and the concept of opportunity cost, each of which is developed in its own lesson. The role of scarcity here is to be the root cause: it is the reason choices must be made at all.

collegeVersion.heading: The factors of production
collegeVersion.body: The limited resources that scarcity refers to are called the factors of production, the building blocks an economy uses to make everything else. Economists group them into four categories. Land covers natural resources: not only physical land but anything that comes from it, such as water, oil, timber, and minerals, whether renewable like forests or non-renewable like natural gas. Labor is the human effort, physical and mental, that goes into production, from the cook in a kitchen to the engineer designing a bridge. Capital means the tools, machines, and buildings people use to produce other goods and services, such as computers, delivery vans, or a factory's assembly line; note that this is physical capital, not money. Entrepreneurship is the work of combining land, labor, and capital in new ways to produce goods and services and bear the risk of doing so. Each factor earns a characteristic payment: land earns rent, labor earns wages, capital earns interest, and entrepreneurship earns profit. A common trap is to call money a factor of production. Money is not itself a productive resource; it is a claim used to buy the real factors. You cannot build a house out of dollar bills, but you can use dollars to hire labor and buy lumber. Because each of these factors is finite, the goods and services made from them are finite too, which is precisely where scarcity comes from.

collegeVersion.heading: Scarcity is not the same as a shortage
collegeVersion.body: One of the most common confusions in introductory economics is treating scarcity and shortage as synonyms. They are different in both scale and duration. Scarcity is permanent and universal: it describes the general condition that resources are limited relative to wants, and it never goes away, in good times or bad. A shortage is a specific, temporary market condition. In supply-and-demand terms, a shortage (also called excess demand) occurs when the price of a good sits below its equilibrium level, so the quantity buyers want to purchase exceeds the quantity sellers offer. Shortages tend to correct themselves: when buyers compete for a limited quantity, sellers raise the price, which both cools demand and encourages more supply until the market clears. Empty shelves during a sudden surge in demand are a shortage, not scarcity; once production catches up or the price adjusts, the shelves refill. Scarcity, by contrast, is still there even when every store is fully stocked, because the underlying resources remain limited. A useful test: a shortage is defined at a particular price and can be resolved by market adjustment or more production, while scarcity persists no matter what the price is or how much we produce.

collegeVersion.heading: Even 'free' things involve scarcity
collegeVersion.body: It is tempting to think scarcity applies only to things that cost money, but that misses the point. Many goods that feel free still draw on limited resources. A 'free' concert in a public park uses land, performers' labor, and equipment that could have been used elsewhere; a free mobile app still consumes engineers' time and server capacity. The clearest example is time itself, which is often described as the ultimate scarce resource: everyone gets the same twenty-four hours, and spending an hour one way means it is gone for every other use. Even air, usually abundant enough to ignore, becomes scarce when clean air is limited. Because almost everything worth having is scarce in this sense, using it always means giving up an alternative use, an idea the opportunity cost lesson develops in full. The takeaway for this lesson is narrower: scarcity is not about whether you paid a price, but about whether the resource is limited relative to the ways people would like to use it. Almost always, it is.

vocabulary.definition: The basic economic condition in which limited resources are not enough to satisfy unlimited or competing wants, forcing choices to be made.
The economy's productive resources, grouped as land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship, that are combined to make goods and services.
Natural resources used in production, including physical land and anything drawn from it, such as water, minerals, oil, and timber.
The physical and mental human effort applied to producing goods and services; its payment is wages.
The tools, machines, equipment, and buildings people use to produce other goods and services; this means physical capital, not money.
The activity of combining land, labor, and capital in new ways to produce output and bear the associated risk; its payment is profit.
A temporary market situation, also called excess demand, in which the quantity buyers want at the current price exceeds the quantity offered for sale.
The idea that people's collective desires for goods, services, and resources are effectively without limit and can never be fully satisfied.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Imagine you have only ten dollars but you want a book, a burger, a movie ticket, and a toy that together cost thirty. You simply cannot buy them all, so you have to pick and leave some behind. Scarcity is that same squeeze, but for everyone and everything at once: the world has only so much land, so many workers, so many tools and hours, while people always want more than that can make. Because there is never enough for every want, someone always has to decide what gets made and what gets skipped. That is the whole reason economics exists, to study how people make those decisions.
eli10.analogy: Scarcity is like packing one small backpack for a trip. The bag only holds so much, but you have more things you would like to bring than will ever fit, so every item you pack means another item you leave on the bed.
eli10.analogyLimits: The backpack makes scarcity look like a one-time packing job you finish and forget, but real scarcity never ends and covers the whole economy at once. A backpack can also be swapped for a bigger one, while the world cannot simply grab unlimited extra land, workers, or hours.

workedExample: A city has one empty lot and a fixed budget this year. Residents want a playground, a parking garage, a community garden, and a clinic on that same lot. Only one can be built, so the lot and the budget are scarce relative to the competing wants. The council debates and picks the clinic. Notice what scarcity did here: it did not tell anyone which choice was right, it simply forced a choice by making it impossible to have all four. The land, the money, and the construction workers are all limited factors of production, and committing them to the clinic means the playground, garage, and garden go unbuilt this year. This is scarcity in action, and it is also the doorway to opportunity cost, which measures what the city gave up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating scarcity as a temporary problem that better planning or more production could permanently solve.
commonMistakes.correction: Scarcity is permanent and universal. Producing more can ease specific wants, but resources stay limited relative to unlimited wants, so scarcity never disappears.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using 'scarcity' and 'shortage' interchangeably.
commonMistakes.correction: A shortage is a temporary market condition at a given price where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied; it can be resolved. Scarcity is the permanent, economy-wide gap between limited resources and unlimited wants.

commonMistakes.mistake: Counting money as a factor of production.
commonMistakes.correction: The factors are land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship. Money is a claim used to buy those real resources, not a productive resource itself.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing that free goods are exempt from scarcity.
commonMistakes.correction: Even things that carry no price tag use limited resources such as time, labor, or land, so they are still scarce and still involve giving up alternative uses.

compareContrast.distinction: Scarcity is a permanent, universal condition of limited resources against unlimited wants; a shortage is a temporary, price-specific market situation where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and can be corrected.
Capital is the physical tools, machines, and buildings used to produce goods; money is a medium of exchange used to buy those real factors and is not itself a factor of production.

keyTakeaway: Scarcity is the permanent gap between limited resources and unlimited wants, and because it can never be erased, it forces every person and society to choose, which is the reason economics exists as a field of study.

questionBank.prompt: In economics, scarcity is best defined as which of the following?
options: A sudden drop in the supply of a single product after a natural disaster
A government decision to ration a good during an emergency
The condition that limited resources cannot satisfy unlimited or competing wants
A situation where sellers set prices too high for buyers to afford
questionBank.explanation: Scarcity is the fundamental condition that resources are limited while wants are effectively unlimited, so not all wants can be met. The other options describe temporary or specific market events, not the permanent, universal condition of scarcity.
questionBank.skill: Defining scarcity as the core economic problem

questionBank.prompt: A city has one vacant lot and a set budget, but residents want a park, a parking garage, and a clinic there. Because only one can be built, the city must choose. This situation most directly illustrates that scarcity does what?
options: Forces a choice among competing uses of limited resources
Guarantees that the most profitable option will be selected
Disappears once the city approves its annual budget
Only affects private businesses, not local governments
questionBank.explanation: Because the lot and budget are limited relative to competing wants, scarcity forces a choice, though it does not dictate which choice is correct. It does not guarantee a profit-maximizing pick, it does not vanish with a budget, and it applies to governments as well as firms and individuals.
questionBank.skill: Applying scarcity to an everyday allocation decision

questionBank.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the four factors of production?
options: Land
Labor
Entrepreneurship
Money
questionBank.explanation: The four factors of production are land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship. Money is not a factor; it is a claim used to purchase the real productive resources. You cannot build with dollar bills, but you can use them to hire labor and buy materials.
questionBank.skill: Identifying the factors of production

questionBank.prompt: During a sudden surge in demand, stores sell out of hand sanitizer and shelves stay empty for weeks until production catches up. How should this be classified?
options: As scarcity, because the resource is permanently limited
As a shortage, a temporary market condition that can be resolved
As proof that scarcity does not apply to consumer goods
As a surplus, because demand exceeded supply
questionBank.explanation: Empty shelves that refill once supply catches up describe a shortage, a temporary condition where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price. Scarcity is the permanent, economy-wide limit on resources and persists even when shelves are full; a surplus is the opposite of a shortage.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing a shortage from scarcity in a real scenario

questionBank.prompt: A student says a free outdoor concert in a public park proves that some things escape scarcity entirely. What is the best economic response?
options: The student is correct, because anything with no price is outside economics
The concert avoids scarcity only because the government funded it
The concert still uses scarce resources such as land, labor, and time, so scarcity still applies
Scarcity applies only to goods that are bought and sold in stores
questionBank.explanation: A zero price does not remove scarcity. The concert consumes limited land, performers' labor, equipment, and everyone's time, all of which could have been used otherwise. Scarcity is about whether resources are limited relative to wants, not about whether a price was paid.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing that free goods still involve scarce resources

title: Choice and Tradeoffs
in30Seconds: Because resources are limited but wants are not, no one can have everything. So every person, business, and society has to choose. And every choice carries a tradeoff: saying yes to one thing means saying no to something else. Economics starts here, with the simple fact that choosing is unavoidable and that each choice quietly costs you the alternatives you passed up.
whyItMatters: Choice and tradeoffs are the doorway to all of economics. Once you see that scarcity forces choices and that choices have costs, the rest of the subject, from prices to policy, follows as careful bookkeeping of what is given up. Academically, this framing underlies supply and demand, the production possibilities frontier, and cost-benefit analysis. Practically, it sharpens ordinary decisions: how to spend an evening, whether a purchase is worth it, how a government should split a fixed budget. Looking ahead, every richer tool you will meet, opportunity cost, marginal thinking, and incentives, is just a more precise way of asking the same question: given that I cannot do everything, what is this choice really costing me?
learningObjectives: Explain why scarcity forces individuals, firms, and societies to choose
Define a tradeoff and distinguish it from opportunity cost
Describe how the production possibilities frontier pictures society's tradeoffs
Apply cost-benefit reasoning to identify a rational choice
Analyze a real situation to name the tradeoff and the single next-best alternative given up

collegeVersion.heading: Scarcity is why we must choose
collegeVersion.body: Economics begins with a stubborn fact: the things people want add up to more than the resources available to produce them. Time, money, labor, land, and raw materials are all finite, while human wants are effectively unlimited. Economists call this condition scarcity, and it applies to everyone. A student has only so many hours in a day. A company has only so many workers and machines. A country has only so much land, labor, and capital. Because none of them can have everything at once, each must decide what to pursue and what to leave aside. That act of deciding is choice, and it is not optional. Even doing nothing is a choice, because the time spent doing nothing could have gone to something else. The scarcity itself is the subject of its own lesson; here the point is simply that scarcity is the reason choice exists. Remove scarcity and economics would largely dissolve, because there would be no need to decide among competing uses of resources.

collegeVersion.heading: Every choice is a tradeoff
collegeVersion.body: Since resources are limited, choosing to use them one way means they are not available for another. This is a tradeoff: to get more of one thing you desire, you give up some of another thing you also desire. A tradeoff is the general shape of every decision, the fact that yes to one option is no to the others. Spend Saturday hiking and you cannot spend that same Saturday earning a paycheck or catching up on sleep. Put a factory's hours toward making chairs and those hours cannot also make tables. Direct a national budget toward defense and there is less left for schools or parks. The tradeoff is not a sign that something has gone wrong; it is the ordinary structure of decision-making under scarcity. Recognizing the tradeoff is the first honest step in any choice, because it forces you to look at what leaves the table when something else is placed on it.

collegeVersion.heading: Tradeoff versus opportunity cost
collegeVersion.body: It is easy to blur two ideas that are closely related but not identical. A tradeoff describes everything you give up in a general sense when you commit to a choice. Opportunity cost is more specific: it is the value of the single next-best alternative, the one option you would most have wanted if you had not chosen what you did. Suppose you have one free evening and three ways to spend it: study for an exam, work a paid shift, or see friends. Choosing to study involves a tradeoff against both other options, but your opportunity cost is only the value of the one you would otherwise have picked, say the paid shift, not the sum of everything you skipped. Keeping these straight matters because opportunity cost is the version economists use to weigh decisions precisely, and it gets its own full lesson. For now, hold the distinction: the tradeoff is the whole bundle you pass up; the opportunity cost is the best single thing in that bundle.

collegeVersion.heading: Picturing society's tradeoffs: the production possibilities frontier
collegeVersion.body: Individuals face tradeoffs, and so do whole economies. Economists draw a simple picture of a society's tradeoffs called the production possibilities frontier, or PPF. Imagine a country that can make only two things, say healthcare and education, using its fixed supply of workers and equipment. The PPF is the boundary showing the most of both it can produce at once. Because resources are limited, that boundary slopes downward: to produce more healthcare, the country must pull resources away from education, so it ends up with less education. A point on the frontier is productively efficient, meaning you cannot get more of one good without accepting less of the other. A point inside the frontier signals waste, resources sitting idle that could have produced more of something. The PPF is worth naming here because it turns the abstract idea of a tradeoff into a line you can see, and its slope is exactly the tradeoff between the two goods. The deeper machinery, how to read the slope as opportunity cost and why the curve usually bows outward, belongs to the opportunity-cost and production lessons; treat the PPF here as a mental image of scarcity and choice at the scale of a whole society.

collegeVersion.heading: Choosing well: weighing costs against benefits
collegeVersion.body: If every choice has a cost, how does anyone choose well? Economists model decision-makers as rational, meaning they weigh the expected benefits of an option against its costs, including the opportunity cost of what they give up, and go ahead when the benefit is worth more to them than the cost. This is cost-benefit reasoning, and it is quieter than it sounds; people do it informally all the time when they ask whether something is worth it. Rational here is a narrow, technical word. It does not mean selfish, and it does not mean the person is always right. A rational chooser can have generous goals, can lack full information, and can turn out to be mistaken after the fact. The claim is only that, given what they know and value, they compare benefits to costs rather than ignoring the tradeoff. Later lessons refine this by looking at decisions at the margin, one small step at a time, but the core habit begins here: name the benefit, name the cost including what you give up, and choose when the benefit wins.

vocabulary.definition: The condition in which people's wants for goods, services, and resources exceed the amount available, so not every want can be met.
The act of selecting one use of limited resources over other possible uses; scarcity makes choosing unavoidable.
What must be given up when a choice is made; because resources are limited, gaining more of one thing means having less of another.
The value of the single next-best alternative that is given up when a choice is made (developed fully in its own lesson).
A model showing the combinations of two goods a society can produce with its limited resources; its downward slope represents the tradeoff between the goods.
A situation, shown by any point on the PPF, in which it is impossible to produce more of one good without producing less of another.
Choosing by weighing the expected benefits of an option against its costs, including opportunity cost, and acting when the benefit outweighs the cost.
The practice of comparing what an option is worth against what it costs, including what is given up, to decide whether it is worthwhile.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: You can't do everything, because you run out of time, money, or stuff. So you have to pick. And every time you pick one thing, you're also un-picking the other things you could have done instead. That un-picked part is the cost of your choice, even when you didn't hand over any money. Grown-ups, businesses, and whole countries all live with the same rule: pick this, lose that. Smart choosing just means checking whether the thing you're picking is worth more to you than the best thing you're giving up.
eli10.analogy: Choosing is like having one plate at a buffet. The plate only holds so much, so every scoop of one dish is a scoop you can't take of another. Loading up on pizza means less room for the tacos you also wanted. You didn't 'lose' the tacos to anyone; you traded them away by filling the plate with pizza. The tacos you most wanted are what that pizza really cost you.
eli10.analogyLimits: The buffet makes the tradeoff visible, but it hides some things. Real choices are rarely just two dishes, and the 'plate' can be time or attention, not space. It also suggests every option is equally available and known in advance, while real decisions often involve uncertainty, changing prices, and the fact that you can sometimes come back for more later, which a single plate does not capture.

workedExample: Maya has one free Saturday. She lists three things she genuinely wants to do: hike a nearby trail, pick up an eight-hour shift that pays 120 dollars, or spend the day resting. She can only do one, which is the scarcity at work. She chooses the hike. Naming the tradeoff, by hiking she gives up both the paid shift and the rest day. Naming the opportunity cost, she asks which single option she would have chosen if not the hike; she decides it would have been the paid shift, so her opportunity cost is the 120 dollars and the experience that shift would have given her, not the rest day too. Was the choice rational? Maya judges that a day outdoors is worth more to her right now than 120 dollars, so by cost-benefit reasoning the hike clears the bar. Notice she never spent a dollar to 'lose' the shift; the cost was the best alternative she waved off.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating tradeoff and opportunity cost as the same thing.
commonMistakes.correction: A tradeoff is everything you give up in general when you choose; opportunity cost is narrower, the value of only the single next-best alternative you passed up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking that only money-tight or poor people face tradeoffs.
commonMistakes.correction: Scarcity includes time and attention, not just money. Even someone with unlimited cash has a finite day, so everyone chooses and everyone faces tradeoffs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing a choice that costs no money has no cost at all.
commonMistakes.correction: Every choice has an opportunity cost, the best alternative given up, even when nothing is paid. A free afternoon spent one way still costs the next-best way to spend it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming any feasible level of production is efficient.
commonMistakes.correction: Only points on the production possibilities frontier are productively efficient. A point inside the frontier means resources are idle and more could have been produced.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading 'rational' as selfish or as always correct.
commonMistakes.correction: Rational here means weighing perceived benefits against costs given available information. A rational chooser can be generous, can lack information, and can still be wrong after the fact.

compareContrast.distinction: A tradeoff is the whole set of things given up by a choice; opportunity cost is the value of just the single next-best alternative within that set.
On the frontier, production is efficient and more of one good requires less of another; inside the frontier, resources are wasted and more of both is still possible.
Scarcity is the underlying condition (wants exceed resources); choice is the response it forces (deciding which wants to pursue).

keyTakeaway: Scarcity makes choosing unavoidable, and every choice is a tradeoff that costs you the best alternative you gave up; choosing well means weighing an option's benefit against that cost.

questionBank.prompt: When economists say that every choice involves a tradeoff, what do they mean?
options: The single most valuable alternative a person gives up
The fact that getting more of one thing requires giving up something else
A situation in which resources are unlimited
The money price printed on a good
questionBank.explanation: A tradeoff is the general fact that, under scarcity, choosing more of one thing means having less of another. Option A describes opportunity cost specifically, not a tradeoff in general. Option C is the opposite of scarcity, which is what creates tradeoffs. Option D confuses a tradeoff with a market price.
questionBank.skill: Defining a tradeoff

questionBank.prompt: Why must every individual, firm, and society make choices?
options: Because resources are scarce relative to wants
Because governments require choices by law
Because prices always rise over time
Because people are naturally selfish
questionBank.explanation: Choice is forced by scarcity: wants exceed the resources available to satisfy them, so decision-makers must select among alternatives. The other options are not the reason choice exists; laws, inflation, and motives do not create the underlying need to choose.
questionBank.skill: Linking scarcity to the need for choice

questionBank.prompt: Maya has one free Saturday. She could hike, work a paid shift, or catch up on sleep. She decides to hike. What is her opportunity cost?
options: All three activities combined
Nothing, because the hike itself is free
The value of the single next-best activity she gave up, such as the paid shift
The money she spent on hiking gear
questionBank.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the one next-best alternative given up, not the sum of everything skipped, so A is wrong. B ignores that a no-cost activity still has an opportunity cost. D describes an out-of-pocket expense, not the foregone alternative. The paid shift is the best option she waved off.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing opportunity cost from the full tradeoff in a scenario

questionBank.prompt: A society is producing at a point on its downward-sloping production possibilities frontier. What does that slope tell you?
options: The society can produce unlimited amounts of both goods
The society is wasting some of its resources
The society's resources have grown over time
To produce more of one good, the society must produce less of the other
questionBank.explanation: The downward slope represents the tradeoff between the two goods: on the frontier, more of one requires less of the other. A contradicts the limits the PPF depicts. B describes a point inside the frontier, not on it. C would be shown by the whole frontier shifting outward, not by its slope.
questionBank.skill: Interpreting the PPF slope as a tradeoff

questionBank.prompt: According to the lesson, a rational decision-maker chooses to take an action when:
options: The expected benefit is greater than the cost, including the opportunity cost
The action is simply the cheapest option available
Someone else recommends the action
The action involves no tradeoff at all
questionBank.explanation: Rational decision-making means weighing benefits against costs, including opportunity cost, and acting when the benefit wins. B ignores benefits and treats price alone as decisive. C substitutes another person's judgment for cost-benefit reasoning. D is impossible under scarcity, where every choice involves a tradeoff.

title: Opportunity Cost
in30Seconds: Every choice has a cost, and it is not just the money you hand over. Opportunity cost is the value of the single next-best thing you give up to get what you chose. If you spend an evening at a concert instead of working the shift or tutoring, the cost is whichever one of those you would most have wanted, not both added together. It applies to time and resources as much as to cash, and it is why economists say there is no free lunch.
whyItMatters: Opportunity cost is the hinge that turns everyday decisions into economic reasoning. It forces you to price the alternatives you cannot see on a receipt: the salary forgone to attend college, the interest given up by holding cash, the hour of study lost to a shift. Businesses that ignore it can post an accounting profit while actually losing money once the value of owner-supplied labor and capital is counted. Policymakers weighing healthcare against education, or defense against infrastructure, are choosing points on a production possibilities frontier where more of one thing means less of another. Learning to name the next-best alternative you surrender is the first habit that separates careful decision-making from wishful thinking.
learningObjectives: Define opportunity cost as the value of the next-best alternative forgone
Explain why only the single most valuable forgone option counts, not the sum of all alternatives
Distinguish explicit costs from implicit costs and connect implicit costs to opportunity cost
Apply opportunity cost to a numeric choice involving money and time
Analyze how the production possibilities frontier and its bowed shape express increasing opportunity cost

collegeVersion.heading: The core idea: what you give up, valued at the best alternative
collegeVersion.body: Scarcity means resources are limited while wants are not, so choosing one thing always means not choosing something else. Opportunity cost names the value of that something else. Precisely, it is the value of the next-best alternative you give up when you make a choice. The word 'next-best' is doing real work. Suppose a free afternoon could be spent working, tutoring, or watching a film, and you pick the film. Your opportunity cost is not the combined value of working and tutoring; it is whichever single option you would have chosen had the film been unavailable. Only the top-ranked forgone alternative counts, because you could only ever have done one other thing with that afternoon. This is why economists insist that the cost of a decision is rarely captured by its price tag alone. Buying a burger for two dollars might really 'cost' the four bus tickets you could have bought instead; the relevant cost is expressed in the best thing that two dollars, or that afternoon, could otherwise have done.

collegeVersion.heading: Explicit and implicit costs
collegeVersion.body: Costs come in two flavors, and both are opportunity costs once you look closely. Explicit costs are out-of-pocket payments, the actual dollars that leave your hands: wages a firm pays employees, rent on an office, the price of a smoothie. Implicit costs are subtler; they are the opportunity cost of using resources you already own. If an owner works full-time in her own shop without drawing a salary, the salary she could have earned elsewhere is an implicit cost. If she runs the business out of a building she owns, the rent she could have collected from a tenant is an implicit cost. Neither shows up on a bank statement, but both are real sacrifices. This distinction reshapes what 'profit' means. Accounting profit is total revenue minus explicit costs, the difference between dollars in and dollars out. Economic profit subtracts both explicit and implicit costs. A business can therefore report an accounting profit while suffering an economic loss, because the owner's forgone salary and forgone rent were never entered in the books. Thinking in opportunity costs means always asking what the resource could have earned in its next-best use.

collegeVersion.heading: Money, time, and resources
collegeVersion.body: Opportunity cost is not a money concept that happens to touch time; it is a trade-off concept that money, time, and other resources all share. An hour is scarce in exactly the way a dollar is scarce: spend it one way and it is gone from every other use. The opportunity cost of a four-year degree is not only tuition and books, the explicit costs, but also the years of full-time earnings a student gives up, an implicit cost that often dwarfs tuition. The opportunity cost of holding a large cash balance is the interest or return it could have earned. Even a decision that looks 'free' because no cash changes hands, such as spending a Saturday scrolling a phone, carries the cost of the best alternative use of that Saturday. Naming the resource and then asking 'what is its best forgone use?' is the general move, whatever the resource is.

collegeVersion.heading: The production possibilities frontier
collegeVersion.body: The classic illustration of opportunity cost at the level of a whole economy is the production possibilities frontier (PPF), sometimes called the production possibilities curve. It shows the combinations of two goods, say healthcare and education, that an economy can produce when it uses all of its resources and technology fully. Points on the frontier are attainable and efficient; points beyond it are currently unattainable; points inside it waste resources. Because the frontier is a boundary, producing more of one good requires moving along the curve and producing less of the other. The amount of the second good given up is the opportunity cost, and it equals the slope of the frontier between the two points. Crucially, the PPF is usually drawn bowed outward rather than as a straight line. This shape encodes the law of increasing opportunity cost: as an economy produces more and more of one good, the marginal opportunity cost of each additional unit rises. The reason is that resources are not equally well suited to every task. The first workers and machines shifted from education into healthcare are the ones best fit for healthcare, so little education is sacrificed; but squeezing out still more healthcare eventually means pulling away resources that were far more productive in education, so the sacrifice grows. Increasing opportunity cost is the whole-economy echo of the same individual logic: every gain is paid for by a forgone alternative, and the alternatives you surrender tend to get more valuable the further you push.

collegeVersion.heading: Where the idea came from, and what it is not
collegeVersion.body: The trade-off logic behind opportunity cost emerged from the late-nineteenth-century marginalist revolution, which recast cost in terms of subjective value and forgone use rather than physical inputs. The term itself is commonly credited to the Austrian economist Friedrich von Wieser (1851-1925), who developed the idea within that tradition; the underlying reasoning is broader than any single author, so it is fairer to attribute the concept to the marginalist school than to crown one inventor. Two boundaries keep the concept sharp. First, opportunity cost is not the sum of all rejected options, only the single best one. Second, opportunity cost is not the same as a sunk cost. A sunk cost is money or effort already spent that cannot be recovered, such as a nonrefundable ticket. Because it is gone no matter what you choose next, it should not enter a forward-looking decision at all; opportunity cost, by contrast, is always about the alternatives still available to you now.

vocabulary.definition: The value of the next-best alternative that is given up when a choice is made.
The single most valuable option a decision-maker forgoes; the one thing they would have done instead of the choice actually made.
An out-of-pocket payment for a resource, such as wages, rent, or a purchase price.
The opportunity cost of using a resource one already owns, such as an owner's forgone salary or forgone rent, with no cash changing hands.
Total revenue minus explicit costs only.
Total revenue minus both explicit and implicit costs.
A curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce given its resources and technology.
The principle that as production of a good rises, the marginal opportunity cost of producing more of it increases, giving the PPF its outward bow.
A cost already incurred that cannot be recovered; because it is unaffected by future choices, it is not an opportunity cost and should be ignored in forward-looking decisions.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: When you say yes to one thing, you are automatically saying no to everything else you could have done with that time or money. Opportunity cost is a way of measuring the 'no.' But here is the trick: you only count the one thing you wanted most out of everything you skipped, because you could only have done one of them anyway. If you had a dollar and could buy either a cookie or a sticker, and you buy gum instead, the cost of the gum is the cookie OR the sticker, whichever you liked better, not both.
eli10.analogy: Think of a TV remote with one screen. Picking a channel does not just turn one show on; it turns every other show off. The 'cost' of the show you watch is the single other show you most wish you could be watching at the same time.
eli10.analogyLimits: The remote makes the cost feel free and reversible: you can flip back in a second. Real opportunity costs are often not recoverable, and the alternatives can differ wildly in value, so choosing well matters far more than flipping a channel. The analogy also hides implicit costs, since a remote never bills you for the shows you missed.

workedExample: Maria has one free weekday evening and three ways to spend it. She could work a shift and earn $80, take a tutoring gig and earn $100, or go to a friend's show that she personally values at $30. She chooses the show. What is her opportunity cost? Line up the alternatives she gave up: working ($80) and tutoring ($100). She could only have done one of them, so her opportunity cost is the single next-best option, the $100 tutoring gig, not $80 plus $100 equals $180. That reframes the decision honestly: the show is 'worth it' only if an evening out is worth at least $100 to her, since that is what she truly surrendered. Notice the $30 is what she values the show at, not a cost; the cost lives entirely in the best thing she declined.

commonMistakes.mistake: Adding up the value of every option you passed on.
commonMistakes.correction: Count only the single next-best alternative. You could have chosen just one other thing, so only one thing is truly forgone.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating opportunity cost as only the money spent.
commonMistakes.correction: Include implicit costs and forgone time. The biggest cost of college is often the years of earnings given up, not tuition.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting a sunk cost drive the next decision ('I already paid, so I must go').
commonMistakes.correction: Sunk costs are gone regardless of what you do next and are not opportunity costs. Decide from the alternatives still open to you.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading a straight-line PPF as the normal case.
commonMistakes.correction: The frontier is usually bowed outward because resources are not equally suited to both goods, so opportunity cost rises as you specialize further.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing the value you place on your chosen option with its cost.
commonMistakes.correction: The value of what you picked measures the benefit; the cost is the value of the best thing you gave up to get it.

compareContrast.distinction: Explicit costs are actual cash payments; implicit costs are the forgone value of resources you already own. Both are real, but only explicit costs appear on a bank statement.
Opportunity cost is about alternatives still available and should shape the decision; a sunk cost is already spent and unrecoverable and should be ignored going forward.
Accounting profit subtracts only explicit costs; economic profit also subtracts implicit costs, so a firm can be accounting-profitable yet economically unprofitable.

keyTakeaway: Opportunity cost is the value of the single next-best alternative you give up, measured across money, time, and resources; on a production possibilities frontier it appears as the bowed-out trade-off between two goods, growing steeper the more you specialize.

questionBank.prompt: In economics, the opportunity cost of a decision is best defined as:
options: The total dollar amount actually paid out for the chosen option
The value of the next-best alternative that is given up
The combined value of every alternative that was not chosen
The benefit received from the option that was chosen
questionBank.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the single next-best alternative forgone. It is not limited to cash actually paid (A ignores implicit and time costs), not the sum of all rejected options (C double-counts alternatives you could never have taken together), and not the benefit of the chosen option (D describes the payoff, not the cost).

questionBank.prompt: A student can spend Saturday hiking (values it at $40), earning $70 at a job, or babysitting for $90. She chooses to hike. Why is her opportunity cost $90 rather than $160?
options: Because the $40 she values hiking at must be added to the job's $70
Because opportunity cost always equals the highest dollar figure available anywhere
Because she gains $90 by hiking instead of working
Because she could take only one other option, so only the single best forgone choice counts
questionBank.explanation: She could have done only one alternative, so her cost is the best one she gave up, the $90 babysitting, not $70 plus $90. A wrongly adds options she could not do together. B states no real rule and ignores that the figure must be a genuine forgone alternative. C is backwards; she gives up $90, she does not gain it.
questionBank.skill: Apply the next-best-only rule to a numeric choice

questionBank.prompt: An owner runs her bakery in a building she owns and works there without paying herself a salary. In economic terms, the rent she could have collected and the wage she could have earned elsewhere are:
options: Implicit costs, which economic profit subtracts but accounting profit does not
Explicit costs, because they are actual cash payments the bakery makes
Sunk costs, because the building and her time are already committed
Not costs at all, since no money leaves the business
questionBank.explanation: Forgone rent and forgone salary are implicit costs, the opportunity cost of resources the owner already owns; economic profit subtracts them while accounting profit does not. They are not explicit (no cash is paid out, so B is wrong), not sunk (they recur with each period's choice and are avoidable, so C is wrong), and they are genuine costs even without a cash outflow (so D is wrong).
questionBank.skill: Distinguish implicit costs and relate them to economic profit

questionBank.prompt: A production possibilities frontier between healthcare and education is drawn bowed outward from the origin. What does this shape reveal?
options: That the economy can produce unlimited amounts of both goods over time
That the two goods have no opportunity cost relationship with each other
That the opportunity cost of a good rises as the economy produces more of it
That resources are equally well suited to producing both goods
questionBank.explanation: The outward bow encodes the law of increasing opportunity cost: as more of one good is produced, each additional unit forces up a larger sacrifice of the other. It does not imply unlimited output (A contradicts the frontier being a limit), and there is a clear trade-off along the curve (B is false). The bow exists precisely because resources are not equally suited to both goods; if they were, the frontier would be a straight line (making D the cause of the opposite shape).
questionBank.skill: Analyze the PPF shape as increasing opportunity cost

questionBank.prompt: You bought a $50 nonrefundable concert ticket last month. Tonight you feel too sick to enjoy it, and staying home would genuinely make you feel better. How should the $50 factor into tonight's decision?
options: It should be added to tonight's opportunity cost of staying home
It doubles in importance because the ticket cannot be resold
It justifies going, since not going wastes the money already spent
It should be ignored, because it is a sunk cost unaffected by tonight's choice
questionBank.explanation: The $50 is a sunk cost: already spent and unrecoverable whether you go or not, so it should not enter tonight's decision. Compare only the alternatives still open, feeling better at home versus a night you would not enjoy. A miscasts a sunk cost as an opportunity cost; B invents a rule; C is the sunk-cost fallacy, spending a bad evening to honor money that is gone either way.
questionBank.skill: Analyze the difference between sunk cost and opportunity cost

title: Marginal Thinking
in30Seconds: Rational choices are made at the margin: you compare the marginal benefit of one more unit against its marginal cost, and you keep going as long as the benefit is at least the cost. The stopping point in the smooth case is where marginal benefit equals marginal cost. Because satisfaction from extra units usually falls, marginal benefit declines as you consume more. Totals and averages can point the wrong way, and money already spent and gone (a sunk cost) never belongs in the calculation.
whyItMatters: Marginal thinking is the engine under most of microeconomics: supply, demand, firm output, hiring, and consumer choice are all applications of comparing one-more benefit to one-more cost. Learning it now means later models feel like variations on a single idea rather than a list to memorize. It is also one of the most transferable habits economics teaches. Deciding how long to study, how many workers to hire, or whether to finish a project you have soured on all become clearer once you ask the marginal question and refuse to be swayed by sunk costs. The people who reason well at the margin avoid two everyday traps: chasing totals when the next step no longer pays, and throwing good time after money already gone.
learningObjectives: Define 'marginal' as the additional benefit or cost of one more (or one fewer) unit.
Explain the marginal decision rule: continue an activity while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost, with the optimum where MB equals MC.
Explain how the law of diminishing marginal utility causes marginal benefit to fall as quantity rises.
Distinguish marginal figures from total and average figures and explain why the marginal figure is decision-relevant.
Apply marginal analysis to a numeric table to select the quantity that maximizes net benefit.
Evaluate a decision involving a sunk cost and explain why past, unrecoverable spending should not affect the current choice.

collegeVersion.heading: "Marginal" means one more
collegeVersion.body: In everyday speech "marginal" suggests something minor. In economics it means something precise: the change caused by one additional unit. Marginal benefit is the extra benefit from one more unit of an activity; marginal cost is the extra cost of that same unit. Economists call the method of comparing these two quantities marginal analysis, and it is the standard way they model choice. The key move is to stop thinking about the whole activity at once and instead ask a narrower question: is the next step worth taking? That reframing matters because most real decisions are not all-or-nothing. You rarely choose between studying zero hours and studying forever; you choose whether to study one more hour. You rarely decide whether a factory should exist; you decide whether it should make one more unit. Once a choice is broken into increments, the relevant comparison is always the benefit and cost of the increment, not of the total enterprise.

collegeVersion.heading: The optimum: keep going while marginal benefit beats marginal cost
collegeVersion.body: The marginal decision rule is simple to state and powerful in use. Keep doing the activity as long as the marginal benefit of the next unit is at least as large as its marginal cost. Stop just before the first unit whose marginal benefit falls below its marginal cost. When the units are small and divisible, this rule points to a clean optimum: the quantity where marginal benefit equals marginal cost, MB = MC. Below that quantity, another unit adds more benefit than cost, so you should do it; above it, another unit costs more than it returns, so you should not. At exactly MB = MC, the last unit is a wash and net benefit is at its peak. This is why economists say rational agents "optimize at the margin." They are not maximizing benefit alone or minimizing cost alone; they are pushing the activity to the point where the two forces balance. Every optimization result you will meet later, from a consumer's best bundle to a firm's profit-maximizing output, is a version of this one condition.

collegeVersion.heading: Why marginal benefit falls: diminishing marginal utility
collegeVersion.body: Marginal analysis only produces an interior stopping point because marginal benefit usually declines as you consume more. The reason is the law of diminishing marginal utility: each additional unit of a good tends to add less satisfaction than the unit before it. Total utility, the cumulative satisfaction from everything you have consumed, still rises with more units, but it rises by smaller and smaller steps. The first slice of pizza when you are hungry delivers a lot; the fifth delivers little; a sixth might deliver nothing. Because the benefit of one more unit shrinks while its cost often stays roughly constant, the two lines eventually cross, and that crossing is the marginal optimum. Diminishing marginal utility is a tendency, not an iron law, and full utility maximization with prices and budgets is its own topic, but the core point for marginal thinking is this: falling marginal benefit is what gives "how much" a sensible answer instead of "as much as possible."

collegeVersion.heading: Totals and averages mislead; sunk costs don't count
collegeVersion.body: A common error is to steer by the total or the average when the margin is what matters. A total benefit can still be rising while the marginal benefit has already dropped below marginal cost; continuing then destroys net value even though the total looks healthy. An average can be flattering or discouraging for units you have already committed and says nothing about whether the next unit pays. The decision-relevant number is always the marginal one. A second trap is the sunk cost. A sunk cost is a past outlay of money or effort that no current decision can bring back. Because it does not change with your current decision, it has a marginal value of zero and should be left out entirely. If a nonrefundable ticket is bought and you would now rather stay home, the price is gone either way; the only live comparison is the benefit and cost of attending from this moment forward. Honoring sunk costs "so they aren't wasted" is the mistake known as the sunk cost fallacy, and marginal thinking is the cure.

vocabulary.definition: Relating to one additional (or one fewer) unit of something, rather than the total or the average.
The extra benefit gained from doing or consuming one more unit of an activity.
The extra cost incurred from doing or producing one more unit of an activity.
The method of making decisions by comparing the marginal benefit and marginal cost of a small change.
Continue an activity while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost; the optimum in the divisible case is where marginal benefit equals marginal cost.
The cumulative satisfaction a person gets from consuming a given quantity of a good.
The additional satisfaction gained from consuming one more unit of a good.
The tendency for each additional unit consumed to add less satisfaction than the unit before it.
A cost already incurred that cannot be recovered and therefore should not influence a current decision.
Total benefit minus total cost; it is maximized at the marginal optimum.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Big choices are easier if you ask one small question over and over: is it worth doing just one more? Compare what one more gives you (the marginal benefit) with what one more costs you (the marginal cost). If the next one gives you at least as much as it costs, do it. The moment the next one costs more than it gives, stop. You usually stop before you run out, because extra helpings feel less special each time. And here's the trick that catches most people: money you already spent and can't get back doesn't count anymore. It's gone whatever you pick, so leave it out of the decision.
eli10.analogy: Think of an all-you-can-eat buffet where each plate takes real effort to go get. The first plate is amazing, so it's clearly worth the walk. The second is good. By the fourth, the food is barely tempting and the walk feels long. You go up for another plate only while the enjoyment of that plate beats the effort of fetching it, and you stop the moment the effort wins. The entry fee you paid at the door never enters the choice of whether to get one more plate, because you can't unpay it.
eli10.analogyLimits: A buffet's benefit falls fast and obviously, but real marginal benefits sometimes stay high for a while or don't fall smoothly, and real marginal costs can rise instead of staying flat. The buffet also hides that in careful economics the units are small and divisible, so the true optimum is where benefit and cost exactly balance, not just the last whole plate you happened to enjoy.

workedExample: Maya decides how many hours to study the night before an exam. Each successive hour adds fewer points because she tires and covers less new material, so her marginal benefits (in exam points) are 10, 8, 6, 4, then 2. Every hour has the same marginal cost: the hour is worth 5 points of forgone sleep and time. Apply the rule, continue while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost. Hour 1: 10 >= 5, study. Hour 2: 8 >= 5, study. Hour 3: 6 >= 5, study. Hour 4: 4 < 5, stop. The optimum is 3 hours. Checking net benefit (total points minus total cost) confirms it: 2 hours gives 18 - 10 = 8, 3 hours gives 24 - 15 = 9, and 4 hours gives 28 - 20 = 8. Net benefit peaks at 3 hours, exactly where the next hour's marginal benefit would first drop below its marginal cost. Notice the total benefit keeps rising past 3 hours (24, then 28) even though studying more is no longer worth it, which is why the marginal figure, not the total, drives the decision.

commonMistakes.mistake: Maximizing total benefit instead of net benefit, and studying or producing more just because the total is still rising.
commonMistakes.correction: The total almost always keeps rising for a while after the margin turns unprofitable. Stop where marginal benefit falls below marginal cost, which is where net benefit peaks.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting a sunk cost drive the choice, e.g. finishing a bad movie or project because you already paid for it.
commonMistakes.correction: Unrecoverable past spending has a marginal value of zero. Compare only the benefits and costs that still depend on your current decision.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading 'marginal' as 'minor' or 'barely worth it.'
commonMistakes.correction: In economics 'marginal' just means 'one more.' A marginal benefit can be large; the word describes the increment, not its size.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the average value of a good to decide whether to get one more unit.
commonMistakes.correction: Averages summarize units you have already chosen. The decision about the next unit depends on its marginal benefit and marginal cost, not on the average.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming marginal benefit stays constant, so more is always better.
commonMistakes.correction: Diminishing marginal utility usually makes each extra unit worth less. That decline is what creates a sensible stopping point.

compareContrast.distinction: Marginal benefit is the gain from just the next unit; total benefit is the sum over all units. The total can rise while the marginal has already fallen below cost.
Marginal cost changes with the next unit and belongs in the decision; a sunk cost is already spent, cannot change, and must be ignored.
Marginal utility is the satisfaction from one more unit; average utility is total satisfaction divided by units. Only the marginal figure answers 'should I get one more?'

keyTakeaway: Decide at the margin: do one more whenever its marginal benefit is at least its marginal cost, stop where they meet, and never let a sunk cost tip the scale.

questionBank.prompt: In economics, describing a decision as being made "at the margin" means the decision maker focuses on which of the following?
options: A. The total benefit and total cost of the entire activity
B. The average benefit per unit already consumed
C. The additional benefit and additional cost of one more unit
D. The lowest possible cost of producing the good
questionBank.explanation: "Marginal" means incremental, the effect of one more unit, so marginal analysis compares the additional benefit and additional cost of that unit (C). Totals (A) and averages (B) summarize units already chosen and do not tell you whether the next unit is worth it; minimizing cost alone (D) ignores benefit entirely.
questionBank.skill: Define 'marginal' as the effect of one more unit

questionBank.prompt: Following marginal analysis, a rational decision maker should keep doing an activity as long as which condition holds?
options: A. Marginal benefit is greater than or equal to marginal cost
B. Total benefit is greater than zero
C. Average cost is still falling
D. Marginal benefit is greater than average benefit
questionBank.explanation: The marginal decision rule says continue while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost, stopping where they meet (A). Total benefit being positive (B) can remain true long after the next unit stops paying; falling average cost (C) and comparisons to average benefit (D) are not the stopping condition, because the next unit's own benefit and cost are what matter.
questionBank.skill: State the MB ≥ MC decision rule

questionBank.prompt: A student gains 10, then 8, then 6, then 4, then 2 additional exam points from each successive hour of study, and each hour has a constant marginal cost worth 5 points of forgone time. How many hours should she study, and why?
options: A. 5 hours, because every extra hour still adds some points
B. 1 hour, because the first hour has the highest marginal benefit
C. 4 hours, because 4 points is still a positive benefit
D. 3 hours, because the fourth hour's marginal benefit of 4 is below its marginal cost of 5
questionBank.explanation: Continue while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost: hours 1 to 3 clear the bar (10, 8, 6 all ≥ 5), but the fourth hour's marginal benefit of 4 is below its cost of 5, so she stops at 3 hours (D). Net benefit confirms it: 8 at 2 hours, 9 at 3 hours, 8 at 4 hours. Studying to 5 hours (A) or 4 hours (C) adds units that cost more than they return; stopping at 1 hour (B) forgoes hours 2 and 3, which still pay.
questionBank.skill: Select the net-benefit-maximizing quantity from a marginal table

questionBank.prompt: You prepaid $40 for a nonrefundable concert ticket. On the night, you feel unwell and realize you would be happier staying home than attending. What does marginal thinking say you should do?
options: A. Attend, because you already paid $40 and staying home wastes it
B. Stay home, because the $40 is a sunk cost and only the benefits and costs from now on matter
C. Attend, because the $40 raises the marginal benefit of going
D. Stay home only if you can resell the ticket for at least $40
questionBank.explanation: The $40 is a sunk cost, gone whether you go or not, so it has zero marginal value and drops out of the decision; compare only the benefit and cost of attending from this moment, which favors staying home (B). Attending to avoid "wasting" the money (A) is the sunk cost fallacy; the past payment does not change the benefit of going (C); and the right choice does not hinge on resale value (D), since staying home is already better on the forward-looking comparison.
questionBank.skill: Apply the irrelevance of sunk costs to a decision

questionBank.prompt: Why does the marginal benefit of consuming more of a good typically fall as a person consumes more of it?
options: A. Because of diminishing marginal utility: each additional unit adds less satisfaction than the one before
B. Because the market price of the good rises with every unit a person buys
C. Because the sunk cost of the good increases with every unit consumed
D. Because average utility is always larger than marginal utility
questionBank.explanation: The law of diminishing marginal utility says each extra unit tends to add less satisfaction than the previous one, so marginal benefit declines (A). Prices are set by the market, not driven up by one buyer's consumption (B); sunk costs are past and fixed, not growing with consumption (C); and while average often exceeds marginal under diminishing utility, that relationship is a consequence, not the cause of falling marginal benefit (D).
questionBank.skill: Explain diminishing marginal utility as the reason MB falls
